title: Labor & Employment: Final Assessment
description: A final assessment covering the key ideas from all three lessons. Reach the passing score to complete the course.

history.note: AI-written question draft. Not yet reviewed by a human (admin); do not give to students.

passing.note: Proposed: 7 of 10 questions (70%). Not approved by a teacher (admin); completion is not recognized until approved.

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: A grocery chain installs self-checkout machines that do much of the work cashiers used to do. Other things equal, what happens in the chain's labor market for cashiers?

choices.text: Labor supply of cashiers shifts left, so the wage rises
Labor demand for cashiers shifts right, so employment rises
Labor demand for cashiers shifts left, so wage and employment fall
Labor supply of cashiers shifts right, so the wage falls

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: In a region's market for bus drivers, labor demand is L_d = 1,500 − 50W and labor supply is L_s = 180 + 60W, where W is the hourly wage in dollars. What is the equilibrium wage, in dollars per hour? (Enter a number only.)
Hypothetical example: A large group of young adults finishes school and enters a city's job market for entry-level office work. Other things equal, what does the labor market model predict?

choices.text: Labor demand shifts right: the wage rises and employment rises
Labor supply shifts right: the wage falls and employment rises
Labor supply shifts left: the wage rises and employment falls
Labor demand shifts left: the wage falls and employment falls

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: A county has 2,500 working-age residents, and its labor force participation rate is 64%. Of the people in the labor force, 112 are unemployed. What is the county's unemployment rate, in percent? (Enter a number only.)
Hypothetical example: During a recession, a car dealership lays off several salespeople because fewer people are buying cars. What type of unemployment does this create?

choices.text: Frictional, because the salespeople are moving between jobs by choice
Structural, because the salespeople's skills are no longer needed
Natural, because some unemployment exists even in normal times
Cyclical, because it is caused by a downturn in the whole economy

questions.prompt: Why do workers who gain more education and training tend to earn higher wages over time?

choices.text: Their skills raise their productivity, so employers value their work more
Training lowers the total number of workers in the economy as a whole
Employers are required by law to pay more for each diploma a worker has
More education raises the legal minimum wage that applies to the worker

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: In a market for farm workers, labor demand is L_d = 700 − 25W and labor supply is L_s = 100 + 35W, where W is the hourly wage in dollars. A minimum wage of $13 per hour is set. According to the simple competitive model, how large is the surplus of labor at the minimum wage? (Enter a number only, in workers.)
Hypothetical example: The equilibrium wage for lifeguards in a town is $16 per hour. The town then sets a minimum wage of $13 per hour. What happens in the lifeguard market?

choices.text: A surplus of lifeguards appears, because the floor is binding
A shortage of lifeguards appears, because the wage falls to $13
Little changes, because the floor is below the market wage
Employment falls, because employers now pay less than before

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: Two regions both raise their minimum wage to $15 per hour. In Region A, typical entry-level wages are already about $16; in Region B, they are about $10. Other things equal, where is a larger drop in hiring of low-skill workers more likely?

choices.text: Region A, because its workers already earn more than the minimum
Both equally, because the new minimum wage is the same $15 in each
Neither region, because a minimum wage affects prices but not hiring
Region B, because the minimum is far above its typical local wages

questions.prompt: Compared with raising the minimum wage, what is a key trade-off of expanding earned-income support for low-wage workers?

choices.text: It raises employers' labor costs, so hiring tends to fall more
It avoids raising labor costs, but taxpayers bear the cost
It replaces wages, so workers have less reason to take jobs
It helps people without jobs more than people who are working
